subject: Career
title: Quantifying Your Impact
description: A quick, practical guide to Quantifying Your Impact.

hook.text: 'Improved customer satisfaction' is forgettable. 'Raised NPS from 32 to 61' is not.

buildup.text: Numbers give recruiters something concrete to anchor on. They create instant credibility.

discovery.text: Even approximate numbers work: 'managed ~$2M budget' beats 'managed large budget.'

twist.text: Not everything can be numbered. For soft impacts, use scale: team size, scope, frequency.

climax.text: The formula: did X, which resulted in Y, measured by Z. Context, action, proof.

punchline.text: If you can't measure it, you can't prove it.

quiz.question: Why are numbers important on resumes?
options: They create instant credibility and anchoring

details.summary: Quantified accomplishments using specific numbers, percentages, and dollar amounts are dramatically more persuasive than vague descriptions of responsibilities. Numbers transform your resume from a job description into evidence of value creation.
details.whyItMatters: Recruiters compare hundreds of resumes with similar responsibilities. Specific metrics differentiate candidates who created measurable impact from those who merely performed a role.
takeaways: Replace vague descriptions with specific metrics wherever possible
Use percentages for improvements and dollar amounts for revenue impact
Even non-revenue roles can quantify impact through scope and efficiency

faq.question: How do you quantify impact when your role does not involve revenue or direct metrics?
faq.answer: Quantify scope: team size managed, projects completed, users served, or processes improved. Quantify efficiency: time saved, error rates reduced, or response times improved. Quantify reach: people trained, documents produced, or stakeholders supported. Every role produces countable outcomes.

faq.question: Is it acceptable to estimate metrics on your resume if you do not have exact numbers?
faq.answer: Reasonable estimates are acceptable if they are honest and defensible. Use language like 'approximately' or 'over' to indicate estimates. Be prepared to explain your methodology in interviews. Inflating numbers is risky because experienced interviewers will probe for specifics.
